The pairings worth acting on are practical ones: aromatic herbs and alliums as scent-based deterrents, and lettuce or spinach as cool-season intercrops that use space and light before broccoli fills in. The well-grounded caution is to separate broccoli from other brassicas, which share clubroot and cabbage-family pests, a rotation and disease principle more than a tested adjacency effect.

beginner: Dill is a classic friend for broccoli. Its strong smell is said to put off cabbage pests, and its flowers bring in helpful insects.
seasoned: Dill works for broccoli through beneficial insects. Its umbel flowers are a magnet for parasitoid wasps and predators like hoverflies and ladybeetles that prey on the aphids and cabbage caterpillars broccoli attracts, and extension trial work pairing aromatic herbs and umbels with brassicas has shown reduced caterpillar damage. Let some dill flower to get the benefit, and site it nearby rather than crowding the broccoli, since flowering dill gets tall and lanky.

beginner: Onions are a traditional neighbor for broccoli; their smell is said to help keep cabbage pests away.
seasoned: Onions are one of the better-supported broccoli companions. Their pungent allium scent helps mask the broccoli and deter the cabbage-family pests, loopers, cabbageworms, and root maggots, that hunt partly by smell, and extension trial work including onion in a mix with broccoli showed reduced caterpillar damage. Alliums are shallow-rooted and undemanding, so they tuck around broccoli without competing for much.

beginner: Lettuce grows fast and low, so you can tuck it between young broccoli plants to use the space while the broccoli fills in.
seasoned: Lettuce and broccoli interplant well on structure and timing rather than chemistry. Lettuce is shallow-rooted and quick, broccoli is taller and slower, so the lettuce uses the open ground and light between young broccoli plants and is harvested before the broccoli canopies over. It is an efficient space pairing; expect a tidy use of the bed, not pest protection.

beginner: Keep broccoli away from other cabbage-family plants like cabbage, cauliflower, and kale. They share the same pests and diseases, so planting them together makes problems worse.
seasoned: Planting broccoli cheek-by-jowl with its brassica relatives, cabbage, cauliflower, kale, Brussels sprouts, concentrates the whole family's shared pests (cabbage worms, loopers, flea beetles, root maggots) and shared diseases in one spot, and repeated same-family planting lets soil-borne problems like clubroot build up. Spread brassicas out and rotate where they grow each year rather than blocking them together.

beginner: Start your seeds indoors where it's about 60 to 75°F. They sprout quickly, in 5 to 10 days, and need bright light right away or they'll get leggy.
seasoned: Start broccoli seeds indoors at 60 to 75°F; germination is fast, usually 5 to 10 days, and seedlings stretch if light is weak after they emerge.

beginner: Plant the seeds about a quarter to half an inch deep in damp seed-starting mix, and keep it evenly moist while they sprout.
seasoned: Sow about 0.25 to 0.5 inch deep into a moist seed-starting mix; broccoli germinates reliably across a wide soil-temperature range as long as moisture stays even.

beginner: Move seedlings outside when they have 4 to 6 real leaves, around 5 to 7 weeks old. Planting ones that are too old or pot-bound can cause tiny premature heads.
seasoned: Transplant at 4 to 6 true leaves, about 5 to 7 weeks old; older, root-bound starts are the classic trigger for buttoning.

beginner: Toughen up your seedlings over about a week before planting them out, and pick a stretch of cool, steady weather rather than just before a hot spell.
seasoned: Harden off over 7 to 10 days before setting out, and choose a cool, settled spell rather than the front edge of a warm-up.

beginner: Space plants about 12 to 24 inches apart, and feed them nitrogen as they grow leaves. Their roots are shallow, so put the food near the plant.
seasoned: Space plants about 12 to 24 inches apart and side-dress nitrogen as the leafy frame builds; broccoli's shallow roots feed best from nutrients placed near the plant.

beginner: Water steadily, about 1 to 1.5 inches a week, while the plant builds its leaves. Letting it dry out or get stressed now leads to poor heads later.
seasoned: Keep moisture even at roughly 1 to 1.5 inches per week through this stage; an early growth check from drought or heat sets up buttoning and loose heads later.

beginner: When the head shows up, keep watering steadily and check it every day. Hot days over about 86°F and warm nights now can make the head loose or cause it to flower.
seasoned: Once the head appears, keep water steady and watch daily; heat above about 86°F by day and warm nights during heading cause bolting and loose, open heads.

beginner: Try to keep the head itself dry when you water, because a wet head in cool, damp weather can rot or get downy mildew.
seasoned: Keep developing heads dry when you water, since wet heads in cool, humid weather invite rot and downy mildew.

beginner: Cut the main head while the buds are tight and green with no yellow, taking about 6 inches of stem. Cutting on time is what makes the plant grow side shoots next.
seasoned: Cut the central head while buds are tight and blue-green with no yellow, taking about 6 inches of stem; harvesting on time is what drives the side-shoot crop.

beginner: Pick in the cool morning and get it into the fridge soon. Broccoli's quality drops within a few days, so harvest close to when you'll eat it.
seasoned: Harvest in the cool of the morning and chill promptly; head quality drops within a few days, so cut close to when you will use it.

beginner: After cutting the main head, keep picking the side shoots while their buds are tight, which brings more. They keep coming for weeks in cool weather, especially on certain varieties like De Cicco.
seasoned: After the main cut, keep harvesting side shoots while their buds are tight to encourage more; production continues for several weeks in cool weather, especially on De Cicco-type varieties.

beginner: Keep feeding and watering while the side shoots keep coming. Once it gets too hot or freezes hard and the shoots stop, the plant is done and you can pull it.
seasoned: Keep feeding and watering through the side-shoot run; pull the plant once summer heat or a hard freeze ends production and quality falls off.

beginner: Each plant gives you one main head about 4 to 8 inches wide, and then a few weeks of smaller side shoots after you cut that main head. How much you get depends a lot on the variety and on the weather staying cool.
seasoned: Expect one central head of roughly 4 to 8 inches across per plant, followed by a steady run of smaller side shoots over several weeks once the main head is cut. Total yield depends heavily on variety and on whether the weather stays cool enough to keep the side shoots coming.

beginner: The big harvest is the main head, which fills out over a week or two. After you cut it, the side shoots come on strongest in the following cool weeks, then slow down once it gets hot or freezes. Some varieties, like De Cicco, are bred to make lots of side shoots.
seasoned: The central head matures across a week or two as it reaches full size, and that is the single largest harvest. Side-shoot production then peaks in the cool weeks after the main cut, especially on side-shoot-heavy varieties like De Cicco and Calabrese, and tails off as heat or hard frost arrives.

beginner: Here's the key thing: cutting the main head while its buds are still tight is what makes the plant produce side shoots, so harvesting on time gives you more overall. It's easy to wait too long and let the head bloom, which makes it less tasty and cuts the side-shoot harvest short.
seasoned: Cutting the central head while the buds are still tight is what triggers the side shoots, so a timely first harvest actually increases total yield. New growers often wait too long and let the head loosen or flower, which both ends the side-shoot run early and gives a coarser main head.

Next time time the crop so heading lands in cool weather, choose heat-tolerant short-cycle varieties for spring, and plant a fall crop that heads as the weather cools.

beginner: You cut the head and found a hollow, sometimes brown space inside the stem. This usually comes from a shortage of the nutrient boron, or from the plant growing so fast (often from too much nitrogen) that the stem can't keep up and splits inside. The head is usually still fine to eat, so it's more about quality than losing the crop. Next time, don't overfeed nitrogen, keep growth steady, and only add boron if a soil test shows you need it.
seasoned: You cut the head and found a hollow, sometimes browned cavity in the stem. This is usually caused by boron deficiency or by growth so rapid (often from heavy nitrogen) that the stem tissue cannot keep up and splits internally. The head is often still edible, so it is more a quality issue than a loss. Next time avoid overfeeding nitrogen, keep growth steady rather than pushed, and correct a confirmed boron shortage with a soil amendment based on a soil test.

beginner: Don't push fast growth with too much nitrogen, and only add boron if a soil test says it's low.
seasoned: Avoid pushing growth with excess nitrogen; correct a confirmed boron deficiency based on a soil test.

beginner: Plant broccoli in spring and again in late summer for fall, in small batches a couple of weeks apart, instead of all at one time. Skip the hottest part of summer, since broccoli will not form good heads in the heat.
seasoned: Broccoli crops in the cool shoulders of the year, so plant in small batches every 2 to 3 weeks within the spring window and again in late summer for fall, rather than all at once. The spring window is short because heads must size up before summer heat arrives, so most gardens fit only a sowing or two before the midsummer gap; the fall planting, heading into cooling weather, is often the more reliable crop.

beginner: Up north, grow broccoli twice a year in the cooler weather at each end of the season. Plant your spring crop a couple of weeks before your last frost date so it makes heads before summer heat, and harvest starting in early summer. Then plant a second crop in mid-July for a fall harvest. The fall crop often tastes better and lasts longer because broccoli likes cool weather, and in the milder cold zones it can give you more than the spring crop. Pick fast-maturing varieties in the coldest areas, and keep a row cover handy to protect young plants from a late spring frost or an early fall one.
seasoned: In the cold zones broccoli runs as two frost-bracketed crops. Set spring transplants out about 2 to 4 weeks before the last frost (roughly late April into May in zone 3) so heads form during the cool, lengthening days before summer heat arrives, then harvest from late June. A second crop goes out in mid-July, timed to head as nights cool in September and October; fall broccoli often eats sweeter and holds longer in the field because cool weather suits it, and in zone 6 to 7 it frequently out-yields the spring sowing. Midsummer is the gap, not a heat exclusion you plant around: nights stay short enough that the limit on both ends is frost, not the day-and-night heat that stalls heading farther south. Lean on fast, short-cycle varieties in the coldest zones, and use row cover at both shoulders to buffer late and early frosts.

seasoned: Cut the central head while the buds are tight, blue-green, and still closed, before any yellow flowers show, taking about 6 inches of stem. Side shoots then form for later picking.

beginner: Before planting, mix plenty of compost into loose, well-drained soil. Broccoli is a hungry plant and likes rich ground.
seasoned: Work plenty of compost into a fertile, well-drained bed before planting and confirm pH is around 6.0 to 6.5. Broccoli feeds heavily and roots shallowly, so a rich, moisture-retentive but well-drained soil pays off.
